title: Extending lifespan: Wear and non-wear component analysis in end-of-life products
author: Ahmed, Bäckstrand, et al.

steps.title: Collect and disassemble BCS
steps.instruction: Gather the end‑of‑life (EoL) brush‑cutting system (BCS) and carefully disassemble it into its individual components (motor, motor‑control unit, wiring, oil tank, chains, screws, chassis, etc.).

steps.title: Categorize components into groups
steps.instruction: Assign each component to one of three functional groups: Group 1 – wear‑and‑tear susceptible parts; Group 2 – non‑wear susceptible parts; Group 3 – electronic aging parts. Note that Groups 1 and 2 together represent roughly 70 % of all BCS components.

steps.title: Clean Group 1 and 2 components
steps.instruction: For every Group 1 or Group 2 component, remove surface contaminants (dust, oil, debris) using an appropriate cleaning method to minimise false‑negative visual diagnostics.

steps.title: Perform 360° visual comparison
steps.instruction: Manually inspect the cleaned component from all angles and compare it with the stored 360° digital representation of a healthy (unused) counterpart in the database. The comparison is performed by an expert; no automated matching algorithm is used.

steps.title: Assess deviation against tolerances
steps.instruction: Identify deviations such as wear depth, edge rounding, leakage, deformation, cracks, or surface roughness. Compare the measured deviation to component‑specific tolerance ranges set for this study:

steps.title: Assign reuse or recycling strategy
steps.instruction: If the deviation is within the tolerance, deem the component reusable and select an appropriate R‑strategy (e.g., recycle or recover for an oil tank at 15 % deviation, depending on material composition). The mapping can be adapted based on the component’s role and safety requirements.

steps.title: Test Group 3 electronic components
steps.instruction: Place each electronic aging component on a functional test‑bed and operate it under realistic conditions to evaluate performance, since visual inspection alone cannot determine functionality.

steps.title: Determine recycling based on composition
steps.instruction: Decide whether to recycle or recover an unhealthy component primarily by its material composition complexity: homogeneous components are generally easier to recycle, whereas heterogeneous components may require advanced recovery techniques.

steps.title: Record findings and perform edge analysis
steps.instruction: Document all inspection results. If any issue is detected, apply edge analysis to enhance representation of wear patterns, material loss, surface roughness, and failure mechanisms, supporting lifespan prediction and quality‑assurance decisions.
